[[Fondaparinux is class one in NSTE-ACS when angiography is more than twenty-four hours away, and class three as the only anticoagulant in primary PCI.]]

A grand test asked which statement is true for a stable NSTEMI awaiting angiography. The key was that fondaparinux causes less major bleeding than enoxaparin. The false options were that heparin is superior to enoxaparin, and that enoxaparin is contraindicated before an invasive strategy.

Now the P2Y12 inhibitor, and your miss.

The stem was an NSTEMI going for an invasive strategy, anatomy not yet known. You chose to pretreat with prasugrel. The key was to defer the P2Y12 inhibitor until PCI. Here's the reasoning, so it doesn't happen again.

Before the angiogram you don't know what this patient has. Some will have disease that needs bypass surgery, and a P2Y12 inhibitor on board means bleeding or a delay. Some will have no coronary cause at all. So giving the drug blind helps only if it prevents events while you wait. Does it? The ACCOAST trial gave prasugrel before angiography. No fewer ischaemic events. More bleeding. Then ISAR-REACT five, which in NSTE-ACS gave prasugrel only at PCI, once the anatomy was known, beat a ticagrelor strategy: death, infarction or stroke in six point nine per cent against nine point three, with no extra bleeding.

[[In NSTE-ACS with early angiography planned, routine P2Y12 pretreatment before the anatomy is known is class three. Give aspirin, and hold the P2Y12 inhibitor until the angiogram. In NSTE-ACS, prasugrel is never given before the anatomy is known.]]

Set the three classes side by side. Aspirin before the lab: class one. A P2Y12 inhibitor before primary PCI in STEMI: class two b. Routine P2Y12 pretreatment in NSTE-ACS: class three. The only softening is when the angiogram is more than a day away. Then pretreatment may be considered, and not with prasugrel.

And once he's on the table for PCI, which one? The European guideline prefers prasugrel over ticagrelor, from that same trial. Then aspirin plus the P2Y12 inhibitor for twelve months, and aspirin alone after that.

Two choices, both set by the clock. One more thing changes the anticoagulant, and you missed it too.

steps.bridge: The kidney changes the dose, not the drug. Now what the 2025 American guideline changed about antiplatelets.

lesson.text:
This is a new card, written for a question you missed. NSTE-ACS, creatinine clearance twenty-four millilitres a minute. You answered that enoxaparin is contraindicated. The key was enoxaparin, one milligram per kilogram, once daily.

Why once daily? Enoxaparin is made of short heparin chains, and short chains leave by the kidney. When the clearance falls below thirty the drug accumulates, the anti-ten-a effect builds up dose after dose, and the patient bleeds. The answer isn't to abandon the drug. It's to give the same dose half as often.

[[Enoxaparin in NSTE-ACS is one milligram per kilogram twice daily. Below a creatinine clearance of thirty it is one milligram per kilogram once daily. Reduced, not contraindicated.]]

The European table adds a floor: below fifteen, enoxaparin isn't recommended at all.

Now place the other anticoagulants around it, because the examiner can swap the drug.

Unfractionated heparin isn't cleared by the kidney. It needs no adjustment at any level of renal function. So when the kidneys have truly failed, heparin is the fallback.

Fondaparinux is cleared almost entirely by the kidney. The European guideline says not below a filtration rate of twenty; the product label says not below thirty. So in your stem, at twenty-four, fondaparinux was the doubtful drug and enoxaparin the adjustable one. That's what made the question hard.

Bivalirudin needs a lower infusion rate below thirty.

{{**Drug** | **Kidney rule**
UFH | no change
**Enoxaparin** | CrCl <30: **1 mg/kg once daily**; <15: avoid
Fondaparinux | avoid if eGFR <20 (label <30)
Bivalirudin | CrCl <30: reduce infusion
Eptifibatide | CrCl <50: halve infusion; dialysis: no
Tirofiban | CrCl ≤60: halve infusion}}

You've already met the last two lines. Eptifibatide is halved below fifty, tirofiban at sixty or below.

And one age rule sits beside the kidney rule, for enoxaparin given with a lytic. At seventy-five or older there's no intravenous bolus, and the dose falls to zero point seven five milligrams per kilogram.

So the kidney changes the dose, not the drug. Now back to the antiplatelets, and what the newest guideline changed.

steps.bridge: Four loose ends remain, and each one has been asked.

lesson.text:
The American guideline of twenty twenty-five mostly agrees with what you've learned. It differs in two places, and those are what an examiner would use. This card hasn't been asked yet, so keep it short.

The default is the same. Aspirin and an oral P2Y12 inhibitor for at least twelve months.

The first difference is how you leave that default early to save bleeding. Once a stent has healed over, most of the protection comes from the P2Y12 inhibitor, and aspirin on top adds mainly bleeding. So the American advice is to drop the aspirin and keep the stronger drug.

[[American guideline, twenty twenty-five: a patient who has tolerated ticagrelor-based dual therapy can switch to ticagrelor alone from one month after PCI, to reduce bleeding. That is class one. The drug you stop is aspirin.]]

The trap writes itself: after one month, continue aspirin alone. That's the wrong way round. The European default is still twelve months of both. It also allows a single antiplatelet, preferably the P2Y12 inhibitor, after three to six months in a patient who is event-free and not at high ischaemic risk, class two a.

The second difference is the choice of drug. The Americans say ticagrelor or prasugrel, with no preference. The Europeans prefer prasugrel at PCI.

On pretreatment the two agree. If angiography in NSTE-ACS will be delayed beyond twenty-four hours, an upstream P2Y12 inhibitor may be considered, and the Americans name clopidogrel or ticagrelor. Not prasugrel. That's your missed question again, from the other side.

Four loose ends remain in this section, and every one has been asked.

steps.bridge: The drugs are sorted. Next the patient without ST elevation: no 120-minute clock, so how soon does he go to the lab?

lesson.text:
Four short situations, each answered by something you already know. Let me give you the stem and you supply the reason.

One. A STEMI patient who gets no reperfusion at all, say he declined it. Which anticoagulant is best? Fondaparinux. This comes from the OASIS six trial, the same one that warned you off fondaparinux in the cath lab. In the patients who had no primary PCI, it lowered death and re-infarction without more major bleeding. Fewer than a quarter got this right; most chose enoxaparin or heparin.

So fondaparinux now has three positions. Class one in NSTE-ACS when angiography is delayed. The keyed answer in STEMI without reperfusion. Class three as the only anticoagulant during primary PCI.

Two. A patient who is vomiting, or has had morphine, and needs P2Y12 inhibition now. You heard the problem in the first hour: opioids stall the stomach, and the oral drug isn't absorbed. Which drug goes by vein? Cangrelor. Onset within about two minutes, gone in about an hour. On a mini test only a third chose it. The rest chose tirofiban or eptifibatide, which are intravenous but act on a different receptor.

Three. Chest pain after sildenafil or tadalafil. No nitrates, for twenty-four hours after sildenafil and forty-eight after tadalafil. You know why.

Four. Troponin in a patient with stage four chronic kidney disease. His troponin is raised every day of his life. So one high value tells you nothing.

[[In chronic kidney disease troponin is chronically raised. Diagnose infarction by a rise or fall between samples, with at least one value above the ninety-ninth percentile, together with evidence of ischaemia.]]

That is the Fourth Universal Definition, which ACS I covered: it's the change that makes it acute. A grand-test question on this was lost by reading a single raised value as an infarct.

That's the pharmacy. You know what each drug blocks, which one to choose, and when to hold it back.

Next, the patient these drugs were mostly for: the one without ST elevation. He has no one-hundred-and-twenty-minute clock. So how soon does he go to the lab?

spine: Clot = platelets + thrombin. Aspirin → COX-1/TXA2 (irreversible, 7–10 days); P2Y12: clopidogrel, prasugrel, ticagrelor, cangrelor; GP IIb/IIIa: eptifibatide, tirofiban (bail-out).
Cangrelor: only IV P2Y12 inhibitor, t½ 3–6 min; the bridge to surgery and the answer when the gut won't absorb.
Prasugrel: contraindicated after stroke/TIA. Ticagrelor: not a thienopyridine; dyspnoea with everything normal (adenosine).
NSTE-ACS anticoagulant: angiography <24 h → UFH; >24 h → fondaparinux (OASIS-5). Fondaparinux alone in primary PCI is class III. Bivalirudin in HIT.
NSTE-ACS, early angiography: routine P2Y12 pretreatment is class III; defer to PCI, then prasugrel > ticagrelor (ESC). DAPT 12 months.
CrCl <30: enoxaparin 1 mg/kg ONCE daily (not contraindicated). ACC/AHA 2025: ticagrelor alone from 1 month after PCI.

questions.text: NSTE-ACS, risk scores and the invasive path

open.text:
Until now the patient had ST elevation, and a clock decided everything. This section is about the patient who doesn't.

In NSTE-ACS the artery is narrowed by clot but not closed. So there's no one-hundred-and-twenty-minute decision, and there is never a lytic, because with nothing occluded a lytic adds only bleeding. The question changes. It's no longer wire or drug. It's how soon to the lab, and risk decides.

[[NSTE-ACS is never lysed. The only question is how soon the angiogram: within two hours for very high risk, within twenty-four for high risk, and during the admission for the rest.]]

So first you'll sort patients into risk groups. Then the two scores that put numbers on risk, GRACE and TIMI, which are easy to confuse. Then the procedure: which artery you enter through, what can go wrong, and when the surgeon takes over.

Most cards here are brisk. Slow down in two places. One is a class: the twenty-four-hour strategy isn't class one any more. The other is surgery, where a grand test asked how long before bypass you stop eptifibatide.

Start with the sorting.

steps.bridge: GRACE above 140 was one of the high-risk features. What goes into that number?

lesson.text:
Three groups, three speeds. The logic is how much muscle is in danger right now.

The very high-risk patient is losing muscle, or his life, as you watch: shock, pain that won't settle, heart failure from the ischaemia, a life-threatening arrhythmia, a mechanical complication, or ECG changes that keep recurring. Each says the same thing: this is behaving like a STEMI. So he's treated like one, with an immediate invasive strategy, within two hours.

The high-risk patient has an active clot but is holding steady: a confirmed NSTEMI, a GRACE score above one hundred and forty, transient ST elevation, or dynamic ST and T wave changes. He gets an early invasive strategy, within twenty-four hours.

Everyone else gets a selective strategy: angiography during the admission, or after a non-invasive test.

{{**Very high risk → <2 h** | **High risk → <24 h**
Shock / instability | Confirmed NSTEMI
Refractory or recurrent pain | GRACE >140
Acute HF from ischaemia | Transient ST elevation
Life-threatening arrhythmia / arrest | Dynamic ST–T changes
Mechanical complication |
Recurrent dynamic ECG changes |}}

Now the class, which is the examinable change. The twenty-four-hour strategy used to be class one. The twenty twenty-three guideline lowered it to two a, because trials of early against delayed angiography showed no fall in mortality overall.

[[European guideline, twenty twenty-three: immediate angiography within two hours for very high-risk NSTE-ACS is class one. Early angiography within twenty-four hours for high risk is now class two a.]]

One of those high-risk features was a score. What's in it?

steps.bridge: GRACE predicts death. The other score is simpler, and it predicts something different.

lesson.text:
GRACE is a weighted score that turns a handful of bedside facts into a probability of death. You'll never be asked to calculate it. You'll be asked what's in it, what it predicts, and the cut-off.

The card lists nine variables, and they fall into two sets. Three from the history: age, previous heart failure, previous infarction. Six from the admission: heart rate, systolic pressure, ST depression, creatinine, raised cardiac enzymes, and no PCI during the stay.

They aren't equal. Age and the haemodynamics carry far more weight than any single yes-or-no item. That makes sense: an old patient who's tachycardic and hypotensive is the one who dies.

What does it predict? The nomogram on this card predicts mortality at six months. The original in-hospital version uses eight variables, including Killip class and cardiac arrest at admission. If an option lists Killip class as a GRACE variable, it's true for that version.

[[GRACE predicts death after ACS. A score above one hundred and forty marks high risk and an early invasive strategy.]]

The one trap is to give GRACE the outcome that belongs to the other score. GRACE doesn't predict events at fourteen days. That's TIMI.

steps.bridge: The patient is sorted and scored, and he's going to the lab. Through which artery?

lesson.text:
The TIMI score for unstable angina and NSTEMI is the opposite design. Seven items, one point each, no weighting. You can do it at the bedside.

Here are the seven. Age sixty-five or more. Three or more risk factors for coronary disease. Known coronary disease, meaning a stenosis of fifty per cent or more. Aspirin use in the last seven days. Two or more episodes of angina at rest in twenty-four hours. ST deviation. And raised cardiac markers.

One of those looks out of place. Why would taking aspirin add a point? Because an acute coronary syndrome that breaks through aspirin is a more aggressive, more thrombotic disease. The trap is the option that says aspirin lowers the score.

What does it predict? A composite: death, new or recurrent infarction, or urgent revascularisation, through fourteen days.

[[TIMI: seven one-point items, predicting death, infarction or urgent revascularisation at fourteen days. GRACE: weighted variables, predicting death. Heart rate and creatinine belong to GRACE, aspirin use to TIMI.]]

You need only the two ends of the scale. A score of zero or one carries about five per cent. A score of six or seven carries about forty-one per cent.

steps.bridge: Radial is safer, but no access is free. What can a PCI do to the patient?

lesson.text:
The wrist, and here's why.

A patient with ACS goes to the lab full of antithrombotics: aspirin, a second antiplatelet, an anticoagulant. The bleed you can most easily prevent is the one at the puncture site. The radial artery is superficial and lies on bone, so you can press on it, and a bleed there has nowhere to hide. The femoral artery is deep, and a bleed from it can track up behind the peritoneum unseen.

So radial access lowers bleeding, vascular complications such as pseudoaneurysm, and the need for transfusion. And because bleeding itself kills ACS patients, it lowers mortality.

[[Radial access is the standard for PCI in ACS, class one: less bleeding, fewer vascular complications and lower mortality. Femoral is for when radial is not feasible.]]

Three trial names go with it. MATRIX, in about eight thousand four hundred ACS patients, showed fewer major bleeds and transfusions and lower all-cause mortality. RIVAL was neutral overall, with fewer vascular complications and a benefit in the STEMI subgroup. RIFLE-STEACS, in STEMI, showed lower cardiac mortality and a shorter hospital stay.

The trap is the option that says radial access reduces bleeding but not death. Two of those trials say otherwise.

steps.bridge: PCI isn't always the answer. When does the surgeon take over, and which drugs must stop first?

lesson.text:
The card sorts the complications of PCI into four groups. Don't memorise the list. Know the two that have been turned into stems, and notice that the access site tells them apart.

The four groups first. Local, at the puncture: bleeding, haematoma, infection, pseudoaneurysm, compartment syndrome. Coronary: dissection, embolism, spasm. Contrast: kidney injury, allergy, and heart failure from the volume load. And others: dissection of the access vessel, stroke, death.

Now the two stems.

Marrow's. Two hours after a femoral catheterisation the patient is hypotensive with back pain. The groin looks fine. That's a retroperitoneal haematoma. It happens when the puncture is above the inguinal ligament, where the artery can't be compressed against the femoral head, so blood tracks backwards and upwards. Back or flank pain, a falling pressure, little to see. The test is a CT without contrast.

The grand test's. Hours after an uncomplicated radial PCI the patient becomes hypotensive, and the ECG hasn't changed. It can't be a retroperitoneal bleed; nobody went near the groin. It isn't stent thrombosis; that would raise the ST segments. So think of what the wire may have done inside the chest. A small coronary perforation leaks slowly into the pericardium and causes tamponade hours later. The first test is a bedside echo.

[[Hypotension after PCI: after femoral access with back pain, think retroperitoneal bleed and get a non-contrast CT. After radial access with an unchanged ECG, think tamponade and get a bedside echo. New ST elevation is stent thrombosis.]]

Three causes of a falling pressure after PCI, and one clue separates each.

steps.bridge: That's the European path to the lab and theatre. Last, where the 2025 American guideline stands.

lesson.text:
Sometimes the angiogram shows disease a stent can't fix, and the answer is bypass surgery.

There are three indications. Anatomy unsuitable for PCI, most often left main or complex multivessel disease. A failed PCI. And a mechanical complication that needs a surgeon anyway, such as a coronary dissection, a septal rupture or a ruptured papillary muscle.

Then timing, which is a trade. Operate in the first days and you put a heart with a fresh infarct on bypass, in a patient full of antiplatelets. Mortality is higher. So for a stable patient the best time is after three to seven days. You operate as an emergency only when waiting is worse: refractory ischaemia, or cardiogenic shock when PCI isn't possible or has failed.

And afterwards the second antiplatelet goes back on, because the grafts don't cure the disease that caused the event.

Now the part the grand tests asked twice: what do you stop before surgery, and how long before? One principle answers all of it. A drug that binds reversibly and is cleared in hours needs hours. A drug that binds for the life of the platelet needs days, until new platelets are made.

Start with the question from your grand test seven. A STEMI patient on an eptifibatide infusion needs urgent bypass. What's the minimum time to stop it? Eptifibatide and tirofiban are reversible and leave by the kidney, so platelet function is back within hours.

[[Before urgent CABG stop eptifibatide or tirofiban two to four hours ahead. Stop clopidogrel or ticagrelor at least twenty-four hours ahead. Aspirin continues.]]

The wrong option there is twenty-four hours for eptifibatide. That's the oral drugs' number. Abciximab, which binds for much longer, needs at least twelve hours, though it's rarely used now.

Then the other stem. An NSTEMI on aspirin and ticagrelor has left main disease and needs urgent surgery. Stop the ticagrelor twenty-four hours before. The wrong options are to continue it until surgery, or to stop it two to four hours before, which is eptifibatide's number put on the wrong drug.

And when surgery can wait, the oral drugs get their full washout.

{{**Stop before CABG** | **Urgent** | **Elective**
Eptifibatide, tirofiban | **2–4 h** | 
Abciximab | ≥12 h | 
Ticagrelor | ≥24 h | ≥3 days
Clopidogrel | ≥24 h | ≥5 days
Prasugrel | | ≥7 days
Aspirin | continue | continue}}

Three days for ticagrelor, five for clopidogrel, seven for prasugrel. Three, five, seven, in order of how hard they hold the platelet.

steps.bridge: That's the uncomplicated infarct. Now the ones that go wrong: the rhythm, the pump, the circulation.

lesson.text:
The American guideline of twenty twenty-five takes a position on six things. You know the reasoning for most of them, some from this packet and some from Shock II. So this is a checklist. It hasn't been asked yet.

One. Complete revascularisation. A stable patient with other significant narrowings does better if they're treated too, at the first procedure or staged, because those plaques cause the next infarct. That was the COMPLETE trial, and it's class one. The exception is cardiogenic shock: there, the culprit only. You met CULPRIT-SHOCK in Shock II.

[[Multivessel disease in a stable infarct: complete revascularisation, at the index procedure or staged. In cardiogenic shock: the culprit artery only.]]

Two. Intravascular imaging to guide the stent: class one in left main and complex lesions.

Three. Radial access preferred.

Four, five and six are the shock positions, and they should sound familiar. A microaxial flow pump is reasonable, class two a, in selected STEMI with severe shock. Routine balloon pump or VA-ECMO is class three. And shock patients belong in a centre with shock expertise. The card calls that last one class one; the guideline's text doesn't clearly grade it, so learn the idea and not the grade.

Europe differs only in strength: complete revascularisation in NSTE-ACS and intravascular imaging are both class two a there.

That completes the uncomplicated infarct: recognised, opened, protected. Now the infarcts that don't go quietly.

spine: NSTE-ACS is never lysed. The question is how soon to the lab, decided by risk.
Very high risk (shock, refractory pain, acute HF, arrhythmia, mechanical complication) → <2 h (I). High risk (NSTEMI, GRACE >140, dynamic ST–T) → <24 h, now IIa. Others: selective (I).
GRACE: weighted, predicts death; >140 = high risk. TIMI: 7 one-point items incl. aspirin in last 7 days; death/MI/urgent revascularisation at 14 days (4.7% → 40.9%).
Radial access is class I (MATRIX): less bleeding and lower mortality. Femoral + back pain + hypotension = retroperitoneal bleed; radial + unchanged ECG = tamponade.
CABG: unsuitable anatomy, failed PCI, mechanical complication; best after 3–7 days. Stop eptifibatide 2–4 h, ticagrelor/clopidogrel ≥24 h before urgent CABG (elective 3/5/7 days).
ACC/AHA 2025: complete revascularisation and imaging-guided PCI class 1; culprit-only in shock; microaxial pump 2a; routine IABP/VA-ECMO class 3.

questions.text: When the infarct is complicated: rhythm, failure and shock

open.text:
So far the infarct has behaved. You recognised it, opened the artery and covered it with the right drugs. This section is about the infarcts that don't behave.

An infarct can complicate in three ways. The rhythm can go, fast or slow. The pump can fail, into pulmonary oedema or shock. And the muscle itself can tear. This section takes the first two; the tears come last.

You aren't starting from nothing. Shock I taught you to read a failing heart, and Shock II taught you every drug and device that pushes on it. I won't teach them again. Here you'll learn only what the infarct adds.

[[Complications by mechanism: electrical, pump and mechanical. Each is asked by its timing after the infarct and by the territory it follows.]]

Listen for three traps. The mechanism of ventricular tachycardia depends on the day: at forty-eight hours it is not re-entry. Heart block depends on the territory, and one bank key gets it wrong. And shock overrides the one-hundred-and-twenty-minute rule. Levosimendan, which you missed twice, appears once more.

Start with the rhythm you should leave alone.

steps.bridge: That's what to do. The bank asked something else four times: the mechanism, and it changes with the day.

lesson.text:
Picture the moment the artery opens. The monitor, which showed sinus rhythm, suddenly shows a wide, regular rhythm at about eighty a minute. The nurse calls it ventricular tachycardia. It isn't.

It's an accelerated idioventricular rhythm. When blood washes back into the territory, the normal pacemaker cells of the Purkinje system speed up, just enough to outrun the sinus node. So you see a wide rhythm only a little faster than sinus, which starts when the sinus slows and stops when it speeds up. It's a sign that reperfusion worked.

[[A wide regular rhythm near the sinus rate just after the artery opens is an accelerated idioventricular rhythm. It is benign and marks reperfusion. Do not treat it.]]

And there's a reason not to treat it beyond its being harmless. Suppress it with amiodarone or lidocaine, and if the sinus node is slow you may be left with no rhythm at all.

How do you tell it from true ventricular tachycardia? By the rate and the behaviour. The idioventricular rhythm runs near the sinus rate and comes and goes with it. Ventricular tachycardia is faster and sustained.

Now the real ones, and the management is a short ladder.

For all of them, correct the electrolytes first. Potassium at four or above, magnesium in the high-normal range. Low levels lower the threshold for every ventricular arrhythmia.

Unstable ventricular tachycardia: immediate cardioversion. If there's no pulse, it's the arrest algorithm.

Stable ventricular tachycardia: a beta-blocker or amiodarone. The beta-blocker comes first in the logic, because early after an infarct the drive is catecholamines. And if it keeps recurring, assume ongoing ischaemia until an angiogram says otherwise.

Non-sustained runs: electrolytes and a beta-blocker, nothing more. They're common in the first forty-eight hours and don't predict later sudden death.

That's what you do. But the bank didn't ask what you do. Four times it asked why.

steps.bridge: That's the fast rhythms. The slow ones follow a simpler rule: tell me the artery and I'll tell you the block.

lesson.text:
This is a new card, because four grand-test questions asked a thing no card states: the mechanism of a ventricular arrhythmia after an infarct. The answer changes with the clock, so build a timeline.

The first minutes to hours. Acutely ischaemic muscle conducts slowly and unevenly, and an impulse can circle back on itself. That's re-entry, and it produces the early ventricular fibrillation that kills before hospital.

The moment of reperfusion. Normal Purkinje pacemakers speed up. That's enhanced normal automaticity, and it's the idioventricular rhythm you've just met.

Twenty-four to seventy-two hours. This is the one they ask. Purkinje fibres and muscle cells at the edge of the infarct have survived, but they're injured and sit partly depolarised. A cell in that state, which is not a pacemaker, starts to fire on its own, pushed by catecholamines and by low potassium and magnesium. That's abnormal automaticity. It gives the ectopics, the non-sustained runs and the ventricular tachycardia of the second and third day.

Weeks to years. The infarct is now a scar with strands of surviving muscle running through it. That's a fixed circuit, and it produces sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia by re-entry.

{{**When** | **Rhythm** | **Mechanism**
Minutes–hours | VF | re-entry in ischaemic muscle
At reperfusion | AIVR | enhanced **normal** automaticity
**24–72 h** | PVCs, NSVT, VT | **abnormal automaticity**
Weeks–years | monomorphic VT | **scar re-entry**}}

[[Ventricular tachycardia or non-sustained runs twenty-four to seventy-two hours after an infarct: abnormal automaticity. Sustained monomorphic ventricular tachycardia weeks to years later: re-entry around the scar.]]

Now see why the question is hard. Re-entry is the commonest mechanism of ventricular tachycardia after infarction overall, so it's the reflex answer. With sustained tachycardia at forty-eight hours most candidates found abnormal automaticity. With non-sustained runs at forty-eight hours a third went back to re-entry. Read the timing. If the stem says hours to three days, it's abnormal automaticity. If it says weeks, months or years, it's re-entry.

Two words separate the automaticities. Normal automaticity is a pacemaker cell firing faster. Abnormal automaticity is a working cell that has no business firing at all.

And the remaining options are there to be crossed out. Early afterdepolarisations belong to a long QT and torsades. Delayed afterdepolarisations belong to digoxin toxicity and calcium overload. Neither is the answer after an infarct.

That's the fast rhythms. Now the slow ones.

steps.bridge: Rhythm is done. Now the pump: when the infarct is big enough to flood the lungs.

lesson.text:
Heart block after an infarct follows the anatomy. So start with the blood supply.

The AV node is fed by the right coronary artery in most people. Below it, the bundle of His and the bundle branches run in the septum and are fed by the septal branches of the LAD. So an inferior infarct injures the node, and an anterior infarct injures the wiring below the node. Everything else follows from which level is hit.

Block at the node, with an inferior infarct. Part of it isn't even damage: an inferior infarct raises vagal tone, and the ischaemic node is bathed in adenosine. So you see first-degree block and Mobitz one. If it does go to complete block, there's a junctional pacemaker just below, which gives a narrow escape at forty to sixty a minute. It responds to atropine, and it usually recovers within days, especially once the artery is open.

Block below the node, with an anterior infarct. To reach the bundles the infarct must have destroyed a large part of the septum. The warning signs are Mobitz two or a new bifascicular block, and then complete block. The only pacemaker left is in the ventricle: a wide escape, slower than forty, and unreliable. Atropine doesn't reach it, and by speeding the atria it can make the block worse. This patient needs a pacing wire.

{{ | **Inferior MI** | **Anterior MI**
Artery | RCA | LAD (septals)
Level | AV node | His–Purkinje
Block | 1st degree, Mobitz I | Mobitz II, complete
Escape | narrow, 40–60 | wide, <40
Atropine | works | does not
Pacing | rarely | often}}

[[Inferior infarct: block at the AV node, narrow escape, responds to atropine, usually transient. Anterior infarct: block below the node, wide escape, no response to atropine, needs pacing.]]

Now the bank, and be careful, because one key is wrong.

A grand test showed block after an anterior infarct and keyed Mobitz one, benign, resolving with atropine. Its own explanation says the opposite. If you meet it again, choose the His-Purkinje level and transvenous pacing.

A second question asked for the true statement, and only fifteen per cent got it. The keyed answer: AV block develops transiently in ten to twenty-five per cent of acute infarcts. The trap was the statement that anterior infarction most commonly produces second and third-degree block. It doesn't. Inferior infarction causes more block of every degree, complete block included. Anterior block is rarer and far more dangerous. Rarer, but worse.

Last, the patient who can't tolerate the slow rate. The European steps are three. Intravenous chronotropes: atropine, one milligram, repeated to three, or epinephrine. The guideline's list also names vasopressin. Then temporary pacing if the drugs fail. And urgent angiography if he hasn't been reperfused, because opening the artery treats the cause.

And a permanent pacemaker? Only if high-degree block persists beyond about five days. Most of these blocks recover, so you wait.

That's the rhythm. Now the pump.

steps.bridge: Wet and warm is treated. When pressure and perfusion go too, it's cardiogenic shock, and the classes matter.

lesson.text:
When enough muscle stops contracting, pressure backs up into the lungs. That's heart failure complicating the infarct, and it comes as two syndromes. Pulmonary congestion, wet and warm. And low output with hypotension, wet and cold, which is shock.

The bedside grading of this is the one new thing on the card. It's the Killip class, and Marrow asked it.

{{**Killip** | **Finding**
I | no heart failure
II | S3 and/or crackles in <50% of the lung fields
III | frank pulmonary oedema (crackles >50%)
IV | cardiogenic shock}}

[[Killip class: one, no failure. Two, a third heart sound or crackles over less than half the lung fields. Three, frank pulmonary oedema. Four, cardiogenic shock. Mortality climbs with each class.]]

Class two and class three are separated by half the lung fields. That's the number a question will move.

The treatment you already know from Shock II, so I'll only remind you of the order.

For the congested patient with a good or high pressure: a vasodilator, non-invasive ventilation, and a diuretic. And remember why the diuretic isn't first when the pressure is high. In hypertensive pulmonary oedema the fluid has been redistributed into the lungs, not gained. High-dose intravenous nitroglycerin and CPAP work in minutes on the real problem. The grand tests asked it twice. Pink frothy sputum, pressure one hundred and eighty over one hundred, saturation eighty-eight per cent, alert: nitrates and non-invasive ventilation. Not a loop diuretic and wait. Not intubation in an alert patient. And at two hundred and ten over one hundred and twenty the first drug is nitroglycerin, not hydralazine and not labetalol.

For the hypotensive patient it reverses. Nitrates are out. A vasopressor for the pressure, and that's norepinephrine. An inotrope for the output, and that's dobutamine. The grand test asked the first-line vasopressor in shock after infarction. Three in four chose norepinephrine, and the lure for the rest was dopamine. You know from Shock II why it lost.

Be honest about the evidence. The European guideline grades these drugs only class two b, because none has ever improved survival. They buy time for the thing that does.

Two more lines from the card. Heart failure in ACS means a longer stay, more mechanical ventilation and more renal replacement. And both syndromes need an emergency echo and an angiogram, because behind the failure there may be a closed artery or a torn structure.

Now follow the cold, wet patient further down.

steps.bridge: Those are the classes. Now one shocked patient, and five decisions in a row.

lesson.text:
Cardiogenic shock in a STEMI means a large territory is ischaemic and failing. Shock II took you through the trials. This card asks only for the guideline's classes, so put them in three tiers by how good the evidence is.

Class one: open the artery. Immediate PCI, or emergency bypass if PCI isn't suitable or fails. This is the SHOCK trial, where early revascularisation saved about thirteen lives in every hundred at six months. And only the culprit artery at that first procedure. Alongside it, also class one: an arterial line, an immediate echo, and early repair of any mechanical complication.

Why the echo so early? Because it separates left ventricular failure from a right ventricular infarct, tamponade, a septal rupture and acute mitral regurgitation. Each changes what you do next.

Class two a: two things. Fibrinolysis, if primary PCI can't be reached within one hundred and twenty minutes and a mechanical cause has been excluded. And the balloon pump, but only for shock caused by a mechanical complication, as a bridge to the surgeon.

Class two b: the things we do every day without proof. A pulmonary artery catheter, inotropes and vasopressors, short-term mechanical support.

Class three: the routine balloon pump. IABP-SHOCK two, six hundred patients, no difference in mortality at thirty days, one year or six years.

{{**STEMI shock (ESC)** | **Class**
Immediate PCI; CABG if PCI fails | **I**
Arterial line, echo, early repair of mechanical cause | I
Lysis if PCI >120 min away, mechanical cause excluded | IIa
IABP for a **mechanical complication** | IIa
PA catheter, inotropes/pressors, short-term MCS | IIb
**Routine IABP** | **III**}}

[[The balloon pump has two classes in STEMI shock. Routine use is class three. For a mechanical complication, as a bridge to surgery, it is class two a.]]

That split comes back in the next section, so hold it. One update: the American guideline of twenty twenty-five lifts a microaxial pump to class two a in selected patients.

The stems are plain. STEMI with shock, door-to-balloon seventy-five minutes: primary PCI, not lysis. Treatment of choice in STEMI with shock: revascularisation.

Marrow added who gets shock and who dies of it. The risk rises with older age, an anterior infarct, multivessel disease, a previous infarct, diabetes and previous heart failure. So if a first, small, posterior infarct presents in shock, something else is going on: look for a mechanical complication or right ventricular involvement. And two blood tests on arrival predict death independently: lactate above two millimoles per litre, and the admission glucose.

Those are the classes. Now run one shocked patient through five decisions.

steps.bridge: That was shock from the left ventricle. One inferior infarct produces shock with dry lungs, and the rules flip.

lesson.text:
An anterior STEMI, cold and wet, in shock. Six bank questions sit on this card, and the first is the hardest in the packet.

The nearest PCI centre is three and a half hours away. Do you lyse or transfer? Two sections ago you learned that beyond one hundred and twenty minutes you lyse. Nine candidates in ten applied that rule here, and they were wrong.

Why does shock change it? Two reasons. A lytic has to be carried into the clot by blood flow, and at a shocked perfusion pressure it works poorly. And revascularisation is the treatment with the strongest proof that it saves lives in shock.

[[STEMI with cardiogenic shock: transfer for revascularisation whatever the delay. The one-hundred-and-twenty-minute rule belongs to the patient without shock.]]

The European guideline does allow a lytic on the way, class two a, if PCI is more than one hundred and twenty minutes off and nothing has torn. So lysing and transferring aren't opposites. But when the options are lyse or transfer, the key is transfer. And when a grand test asks which intervention has the strongest effect on survival in a large anterior STEMI with a pressure of seventy-two over forty: early coronary reperfusion.

Now the drugs, quickly, because Shock II taught them and this card only asks you to pick.

The systolic pressure is ninety-six. Output is low but there's a pressure to work with: dobutamine.

The systolic is below ninety. Now perfusion depends on pressure: norepinephrine first, then add the inotrope. If he's already on dobutamine and the pressure keeps falling to eighty-five over fifty-five, add norepinephrine. Nine in ten got that.

One wrinkle. A DocT question gives chronic heart failure with a systolic of eighty-five and keys dobutamine, where this card would say norepinephrine. The two keys come from different guidelines. Use this rule. Low output with a borderline pressure: dobutamine. Frank shock with a mean pressure under sixty-five: norepinephrine first. And not dopamine as the first choice, whatever an old key says.

Then the patient on carvedilol. The card answers milrinone, because it works downstream of the blocked receptor. That's true. But you know from Shock II what the grand tests keyed, twice, and what you chose instead. When levosimendan is offered, it's levosimendan. Milrinone only if levosimendan isn't there.

One mechanism question belongs here. A drug that raises cardiac output, dilates veins and speeds calcium reuptake into the sarcoplasmic reticulum. Half the candidates chose selective beta-one stimulation or troponin C sensitisation. It's phosphodiesterase three inhibition: milrinone. The reuptake is the clue. That's cyclic AMP at work, and levosimendan doesn't raise it.

And the balloon pump. Not routinely. You have the class from the last card.

So far the shock has come from the left ventricle. There's one infarct where it comes from the right, and there almost everything you'd reach for is wrong.

steps.bridge: Rhythm, failure and shock are done. The third family is structural: the infarct tears.

lesson.text:
An inferior STEMI. Pressure eighty over fifty. The lungs are clear and the neck veins are full. Hypotension with dry lungs and a high venous pressure: the left ventricle isn't the problem. It's the right.

The right coronary artery supplies the right ventricle, and when it's blocked near its origin the right ventricle infarcts along with the inferior wall. You confirm it with a right-sided ECG: ST elevation of one millimetre or more in V4R. Record it early, because that sign fades within hours.

You met the physiology in the first hour, with the nitrate. A stunned right ventricle is a passive conduit. It moves blood to the left side only if it's filled at a high pressure. So the treatment is the reverse of left-sided shock.

First, fluid. A cautious crystalloid bolus while primary PCI is arranged. Cautious, because the two ventricles share a septum and a pericardium. Overfill the right, and the septum bulges into the left and the output falls again.

Second, avoid everything that lowers preload.

[[Right ventricular infarct: clear lungs, raised JVP, hypotension, ST elevation in V4R. Give fluid. Avoid nitrates, diuretics, morphine and beta-blockers.]]

Third, if fluid fails, dobutamine. And protect the atrial kick. Inferior infarcts cause AV block, as you've just learned, and a right ventricle that depends on filling loses a great deal when the atria stop contributing. So if you pace, pace both chambers in sequence.

The bank stem is the one from the first hour, and it's worth hearing again now that you have the whole picture. Inferior STEMI, given aspirin, nitrate and morphine. The pressure falls from one hundred and sixty over ninety to sixty over thirty. Half called it a drug reaction. It's cardiogenic shock from a right ventricular infarct, and two of those three drugs caused the fall.

The discriminator is the lungs. Shock with crackles is the left ventricle: no fluid. Shock with clear lungs and full neck veins after an inferior infarct is the right ventricle: fluid.

That's the rhythm and the pump. One family of complications is left, and it's the one where minutes matter most.

spine: AIVR at reperfusion: wide, regular, near sinus rate; benign, no treatment. VT: electrolytes (K ≥4, Mg), cardiovert if unstable, β-blocker or amiodarone if stable.
Mechanism by timing: early VF re-entry; AIVR enhanced normal automaticity; 24–72 h VT/NSVT ABNORMAL automaticity; weeks–years scar re-entry.
AV block: inferior MI → nodal, narrow escape, atropine works, transient. Anterior MI → infranodal, wide escape, needs pacing. Inferior MI causes more block of every degree.
Killip I–IV: none; S3/crackles <50%; pulmonary oedema; shock. High BP oedema → nitrate + NIV. Low BP → norepinephrine, then dobutamine.
STEMI shock: immediate culprit-only PCI (I), transfer whatever the delay. Routine IABP class III; IABP for a mechanical complication IIa.
RV infarct: inferior STEMI, clear lungs, raised JVP, V4R. Fluid; no nitrates, diuretics, morphine, β-blockers; keep AV synchrony.

questions.text: Ruptures, aneurysm and the long road after

open.text:
The last section begins with the worst days and ends with the rest of the patient's life.

Dead muscle is soft. For the first week, before scar forms, it can tear, and where it tears decides what you see. The bank has asked six questions on that.

[[Three ruptures in the first week: free wall gives tamponade, septum gives a shunt with a loud murmur, papillary muscle gives acute mitral regurgitation. All three end in surgery.]]

If the wall holds but never recovers, it thins and bulges, and that's the aneurysm. Then come the drugs every survivor takes home, which is where your other missed question sits: the ACE inhibitor after an infarct with an ejection fraction of thirty-two per cent.

Listen for one trap above the others. In the rupture questions the examiner asks for the next step, and offers norepinephrine, a balloon pump and surgery side by side. The balloon pump that is class three in routine shock is the right answer here, because a mechanical complication is the exception.

Start with the three tears, side by side.

steps.bridge: Of the three, the septal rupture forces the hardest decision: operate now or wait.

lesson.text:
Take each rupture from its mechanism, and the presentation follows.

The free wall. The ventricle opens into the pericardium, and the sac fills in moments. The heart keeps its electrical rhythm but can't fill, so there's no output. Sudden chest pain, collapse, a rhythm on the monitor and no pulse. The finding is blood in the pericardium with tamponade. Two grand-test stems gave sudden hypotension or pulseless electrical activity days after a large STEMI with tamponade on echo. The answer both times: free wall rupture. It's rare, under one per cent, and the risks are older age, no reperfusion and late lysis.

The septum. Now the hole is between the ventricles, and blood takes the easy path, left to right. The lungs are flooded and the body is starved, so you get rapid heart failure and shock, in the first week. The sign is a new, loud systolic murmur, often with a thrill at the left sternal edge. And if you sample the blood, the oxygen saturation steps up between the right atrium and the pulmonary artery.

The papillary muscle. The mitral leaflet loses its anchor and flails, and the ventricle empties backwards into a small left atrium that has had no time to stretch. Sudden pulmonary oedema, with or without shock. Which muscle? The posteromedial one, because it has a single blood supply, from the posterior descending artery. The anterolateral muscle has two. So this follows an inferior or posterior infarct, often a small one.

And here's the catch. The murmur may be soft or short, because the left atrial pressure rises so fast that the gradient disappears. A quiet heart with flash pulmonary oedema still needs an echo.

{{ | **Free wall** | **Septum** | **Papillary muscle**
Presents | collapse, PEA | failure / shock, days 1–7 | flash pulmonary oedema
Finding | tamponade | loud murmur, O₂ step-up | soft murmur, flail leaflet
Bridge | pericardiocentesis | IABP | IABP, vasodilator
Then | surgical repair | surgery / device closure | mitral surgery}}

[[Septal rupture: loud murmur at the left sternal edge with an oxygen step-up. Papillary muscle rupture: apical murmur, often soft, with flash pulmonary oedema, after an inferior infarct.]]

Now the management, where four of the six questions sit.

All three end in surgery. The question is what you do in the minutes before. For the free wall, pericardiocentesis buys time. For the other two, think about where the blood is going. It has two exits: forward into the aorta, or the wrong way, through the hole or the valve. How much goes each way depends on the resistance of each exit. Lower the resistance in the aorta, and more goes forward.

That's what the balloon pump does. It deflates just before systole and drops the afterload, and it raises the diastolic pressure that feeds the coronaries. A vasopressor does the opposite. It raises the afterload and drives more blood the wrong way.

[[For shock from papillary muscle or septal rupture, the bridge to surgery is the balloon pump, which lowers afterload. Norepinephrine raises afterload and worsens the leak.]]

Here's how the bank played it. An inferior STEMI with a murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold and hypotensive: which intervention? Only thirty-eight per cent chose the balloon pump; most chose norepinephrine. Papillary rupture on echo with flash pulmonary oedema: next step? The balloon pump again, and fewer than half chose it, because valve replacement was sitting beside it. When the stem says next and the balloon is offered, stabilise first. But in a third stem, partial rupture with hypotension, there was no balloon option, and the choices were diuretics and observe, a vasodilator and reassess in forty-eight hours, or urgent mitral surgery. Then it's surgery.

One more, simpler. A posterior infarct, then breathlessness with a new apical holosystolic murmur and crackles. The mechanism is acute mitral regurgitation. Not pulmonary embolism, and not pump failure.

Last, the mortality figures on the card. Free wall rupture, seventy-five to eighty per cent. Papillary muscle, twenty to twenty-five per cent with surgery. For the septum the card says twenty to forty per cent with early surgery. That's optimistic, and the next card tells you why.

steps.bridge: The wall that tears kills quickly. The wall that holds but never recovers causes a slower problem.

lesson.text:
The septal rupture gets a card of its own because of one decision: when to operate. It hasn't been asked, so take the logic and two corrections.

First, where it happens. An anterior infarct tears the septum near the apex, usually a simple hole. An inferior infarct tears it at the base, a more complex defect that does worse. The card says anterior or posterolateral, following its notes. The usual pairing is anterior and inferior, and that's the one to learn.

Now the timing, which is a real dilemma. Operate early, and the surgeon is sewing a patch into dead muscle that holds stitches badly. Wait a few weeks, and the edges turn to scar and the repair holds. But while you wait the hole can enlarge, and the patient can die.

So the patient decides.

[[Septal rupture: refractory shock means surgery now, despite the risk. A patient who stabilises on support can have delayed repair once the edges have scarred.]]

The trap is the blanket rule: wait four to six weeks for every septal rupture. Only for the stable.

The second correction is the number. The card gives twenty to forty per cent mortality for early surgery. In the large surgical registry it was about fifty-four per cent for repair within seven days, and eighteen per cent after that.

And the newer option: percutaneous closure with a device, in selected anatomy.

steps.bridge: The structure is dealt with. What remains is the prescription for life, and one of your misses is in it.

lesson.text:
Suppose the wall doesn't tear. A large infarct that goes right through the wall and isn't reperfused in time heals as a thin sheet of scar, and with every beat that sheet bulges outward. That's a left ventricular aneurysm. It follows fewer than five in a hundred infarcts, fewer still since primary PCI, and it sits where the big anterior infarcts are: the anteroseptal wall and the apex.

The ECG has two features, and together they're the question. Q waves, because the muscle is dead. And ST elevation that never comes down.

[[ST elevation that persists for weeks after an anterior infarct, with Q waves, no new pain and no rise in troponin, is a left ventricular aneurysm, not a new infarct.]]

The trap is to call it re-infarction and send the patient for reperfusion.

That fits into a simple three-way reading of an ECG, which a DocT question tested. Q waves with no ST elevation: an old, healed infarct. ST elevation with symptoms or a rising troponin: an acute one. Q waves with persistent ST elevation weeks later: an aneurysm. The stem gave a patient with known coronary disease, fatigue, and Q waves in leads one, aVL and V5. Fewer than half said old lateral infarction. The rest said acute coronary syndrome. But Q waves are permanent. Acute ischaemia needs ST or T wave change and a story to match.

The main complication comes from stasis. Blood sits still in a pouch that doesn't contract, a thrombus forms at the apex, and pieces travel to the brain and the limbs. The card says long-term oral anticoagulation, and that's the classic exam answer. The current European guideline is more modest: anticoagulation should be considered for three to six months, guided by repeat imaging.

Surgery is for a large aneurysm, recurrent embolism, or one causing refractory heart failure or ventricular arrhythmias.

And one mimic that matters. A true aneurysm has a wide neck, its wall is scar, and it rarely ruptures. A pseudoaneurysm is a free wall rupture that the pericardium has sealed off. Its neck is narrow, its wall isn't myocardium at all, and it does rupture. So it goes to the surgeon.

steps.bridge: The beta-blocker row has a soft cell: LVEF above 40%. Four recent trials tested exactly that.

lesson.text:
The patient is going home. Which drugs go with him, and which of them actually lengthen his life? This card is a grid, and the column that matters is the ejection fraction.

Start with the damaged ventricle: an ejection fraction of forty per cent or less, or heart failure.

After a large infarct the surviving muscle is overloaded. The body's answer is to switch on angiotensin and catecholamines, and over months they make the ventricle dilate and scar. That's remodelling, and it's what kills later. So the drugs that prolong life are the ones that block those signals.

The ACE inhibitor blocks angiotensin and limits the dilatation. Class one.

That's the grand-test question you missed. An infarct, an ejection fraction of thirty-two per cent, and the question was which drug to continue long term for secondary prevention. The key was the ACE inhibitor. It isn't there for the blood pressure. It's there for the ventricle.

[[After an infarct with an LVEF of forty per cent or less, an ACE inhibitor and a beta-blocker are both class one, long term. Add a mineralocorticoid antagonist if there is also heart failure or diabetes.]]

The beta-blocker blocks the catecholamines. It lowers oxygen demand, raises the threshold for ventricular fibrillation, and in the older trials cut deaths by more than a fifth. Class one.

The mineralocorticoid antagonist is the third. Aldosterone keeps driving fibrosis even on an ACE inhibitor. In the EPHESUS trial eplerenone reduced deaths in exactly this group: an ejection fraction of forty or less with heart failure or diabetes. Check the potassium and creatinine first. The card grades it one B; the twenty twenty-three guideline has it at one A.

Now the other column, an ejection fraction above forty. The ACE inhibitor drops to class two a, unless there is diabetes, hypertension or kidney disease, which keep it at class one. So does the beta-blocker, and the next card is about how soft that has become.

Two rows don't change with the ejection fraction. A high-dose statin for everyone, class one. And dual antiplatelet therapy for twelve months.

{{**Drug** | **LVEF ≤40% or HF** | **LVEF >40%**
β-blocker | **I** | IIa
ACE inhibitor | **I** | IIa (I if DM, HTN, CKD)
MRA | **I** (with HF or diabetes) | –
High-dose statin | I | I
DAPT | 12 months | 12 months}}

A DocT question shows the trap. After an infarct, an ejection fraction of twenty-five per cent, stable but breathless: which therapy improves long-term prognosis? The options were a beta-blocker, intravenous milrinone, digoxin and nitrates. Fewer than half chose the beta-blocker. Sort them by one question: does it prolong life, or only ease symptoms? Milrinone raises oxygen demand and arrhythmias and worsens long-term survival; it's a bridge in shock. Digoxin reduced admissions but not deaths. Nitrates treat angina.

[[Drugs that prolong life after an infarct with a low ejection fraction: beta-blocker, ACE inhibitor, mineralocorticoid antagonist, statin. Inotropes, digoxin, nitrates and diuretics treat symptoms only.]]

steps.bridge: One card left: the 2025 American targets for lipids, rehabilitation and haemoglobin.

lesson.text:
The beta-blocker earned its place before stents, when infarcts were large and ventricles were left damaged. Does it still help a patient whose artery was opened within the hour and whose ventricle is normal? Recent trials asked, and the answer depends on the ejection fraction. This hasn't been asked in the bank, but it's new enough to appear.

REDUCE-AMI. Ejection fraction fifty per cent or more. No benefit.

REBOOT. Ejection fraction above forty, no heart failure. No benefit overall.

BETAMI-DANBLOCK. Ejection fraction forty or more. Fewer events, fourteen point two per cent against sixteen point three, mainly fewer new infarctions.

Why the disagreement? The signal sat in the patients with a mildly reduced ejection fraction, between forty and forty-nine. Pooled across the trials, nearly nineteen hundred of them, death, infarction or heart failure fell from fourteen point four per cent to ten point seven. A quarter fewer.

[[Beta-blocker after infarction: clear benefit with an LVEF of forty or below, benefit in the pooled data at forty to forty-nine, and no demonstrated benefit at fifty or above.]]

The mechanism explains it. The drug protects a damaged ventricle from arrhythmia and remodelling. Where there's little damage, there's little to protect.

One caution. Both guidelines were written before most of these trials reported, and both still support a beta-blocker after an infarct. So for the exam it is not a wrong answer. What's wrong is the statement that it improves outcome in every patient.

The last card is the discharge checklist from the American guideline of twenty twenty-five. None of it has been asked yet, so learn the numbers and one exception.

A high-intensity statin for everyone, whatever the starting cholesterol. Then the LDL on that statin decides whether you add a second agent, such as ezetimibe or a PCSK9 inhibitor.

[[American guideline, twenty twenty-five: on a maximal statin, an LDL of seventy milligrams per decilitre or more means add a non-statin agent, class one. Between fifty-five and sixty-nine, adding one is reasonable, class two a.]]

The trap is an LDL of sixty with ezetimibe called class one. Recheck a fasting lipid panel four to eight weeks after any change. And refer for cardiac rehabilitation before discharge, class one, because patients referred later often never go.

Now the exception, and for an intensivist it's the most interesting line in the packet. You transfuse at a haemoglobin of seven. That threshold was never tested in acute infarction, where the muscle beyond a narrowed artery depends on every gram. The MINT trial tested it, and a liberal target of ten gave fewer deaths or infarctions than a restrictive one, narrowly missing significance.

[[In acute coronary syndrome with anaemia and no active bleeding, transfusing to keep the haemoglobin at ten grams per decilitre may be reasonable. That is class two b, and an exception to the general threshold of seven.]]

That's the infarct, start to finish. You recognised it, opened the artery, covered it with the right drugs, managed what went wrong, and sent the patient home.

But look at what he takes with him. A scar, and around it muscle that was ischaemic. You saw in this packet what those do: the scar is a circuit for re-entry, and injured cells fire when they shouldn't. Nearly every arrhythmia you'll meet on the unit begins in one of those two places. So that's next: a monitor, a rhythm that's too fast or too slow, and how to read it.

spine: Days 1–7, necrotic muscle tears. Free wall → haemopericardium, tamponade, PEA. Septum → loud murmur, O₂ step-up, shock. Papillary (posteromedial, inferior MI) → flash pulmonary oedema, soft murmur.
All three need surgery. Bridge for septal/papillary rupture = IABP (lowers afterload, IIa); norepinephrine worsens the leak. No IABP option → urgent surgery.
VSR: refractory shock → operate now; stable on support → delayed repair. Registry mortality ~54% within 7 days.
Aneurysm: persistent ST elevation + Q waves weeks later, no troponin rise; apical thrombus → anticoagulate (ESC 3–6 months). Pseudoaneurysm: narrow neck, ruptures, surgery.
LVEF ≤40%: β-blocker, ACE inhibitor (class I), MRA if HF/diabetes; statin and 12-month DAPT for all. Inotropes, digoxin, nitrates do not prolong life.
β-blocker with LVEF ≥50%: no proven benefit (REDUCE-AMI, REBOOT). LDL ≥70 on statin → add non-statin (1). Hb 10 in ACS anaemia may be reasonable (MINT).

close.text:
So let's walk back through Patient C, from the door to discharge.

You read his ECG in ten minutes, put him on a monitor, and held the oxygen because his saturation was fine. You chose the road by the clock. You covered the artery with drugs that stop platelets and drugs that stop thrombin, and you learned which of them to hold, and when. You watched for the rhythms and the failing pump that follow an infarct. And you sent him home on the drugs that keep the scar from growing.

Now the traps. These are the ones you've actually met.

One. The PCI centre is far away. The tempting cut-off is ninety minutes. [[The choice between primary PCI and lysis is made at one hundred and twenty minutes, from diagnosis to wire. Beyond that, lyse within ten minutes, then transfer.]]

Two. An NSTEMI, anatomy not yet known. The tempting move is to load prasugrel now. Don't. If he's going for early angiography, the P2Y12 inhibitor waits for the anatomy, because he may need bypass surgery instead. You missed this one.

Three. Creatinine clearance of twenty-four. The tempting answer is that enoxaparin is contraindicated. [[Below a clearance of thirty, enoxaparin is not stopped. It's given once a day instead of twice.]] Another grand-test miss.

Four. Urgent bypass surgery, and he's on eptifibatide. The short-acting glycoprotein inhibitors are stopped only two to four hours before. Clopidogrel and ticagrelor need at least a day.

Five. Discharge, and his ejection fraction is thirty-two percent. The ACE inhibitor is a class one drug at forty percent or below, together with a beta-blocker. That was a miss too.

And six. Saturation ninety-five, and someone puts him on two litres of oxygen. Routine oxygen above ninety percent is class three. It doesn't help, and it may harm.

The check comes up on the next screen. Answer each in your head before you tap it open.

And carry one picture into the next packet. Patient C goes home with a scar, and around it, muscle that was starved. Those are the places where rhythms go wrong. So next, the monitor shows you a rhythm that's too fast, or too slow. How do you read it?

drill.q: STEMI, nearest PCI centre 150 km (or 4 h) away. Next step?
drill.a: Thrombolysis within 10 min, then transfer. PCI is chosen only if the wire can cross within 120 min of diagnosis (NEET 2025, Marrow, DocT).

drill.q: What do 120, 60 and 90 minutes each mean in STEMI?
drill.a: 120: choose PCI over lysis. 60: target at a PCI centre. 90: target if transferred.

drill.q: After lysis: when is it judged, what defines failure, and what follows success?
drill.a: At 60-90 min. Failure = <50% ST resolution, ongoing pain or instability → rescue PCI now. Success → angiography at 2-24 h.

drill.q: DES 2 months ago, sudden anterior ST elevation. Management?
drill.a: Stent thrombosis = STEMI: DAPT, anticoagulation, urgent PCI. Not lysis, nitrates, echo or observation (NEET 2025; DocT GT 48%).

drill.q: STEMI in cardiogenic shock, PCI centre 3.5 h away: lyse or transfer?
drill.a: Transfer for revascularisation whatever the delay; culprit-only PCI (9% right).

drill.q: SaO₂ 95% in ACS: oxygen?
drill.a: Withhold. Oxygen only if SaO₂ <90% or PaO₂ <60 mmHg; routine oxygen above that is class III (DETO2X-AMI).

drill.q: Inferior STEMI: BP falls to 60/30 ten minutes after nitroglycerin. Diagnosis and treatment?
drill.a: RV infarct (cardiogenic shock), not a drug reaction. Fluid bolus, V4R, no nitrates, diuretics or morphine.

drill.q: Absolute contraindication to lysis: SBP >180, warfarin, TIA 3 months ago, or previous haemorrhagic stroke?
drill.a: Previous haemorrhagic stroke (absolute, for life). The rest are relative. Ischaemic stroke <6 months is absolute; a known AVM is absolute on every list.

drill.q: Tenecteplase: dose for 72 kg aged 60, and aged 80? Which P2Y12 inhibitor with it?
drill.a: 40 mg single bolus; 20 mg (half dose at ≥75 y). Clopidogrel 300 mg (75 mg, no load, if >75 y).

drill.q: Recent stent on aspirin + clopidogrel, needs urgent surgery. IV bridge?
drill.a: Cangrelor: the only IV P2Y12 inhibitor, t½ 3-6 min. Not tirofiban or eptifibatide (GP IIb/IIIa).

drill.q: Breathless 12 h after PCI; SpO₂, examination, ECG and CT normal. Culprit drug and mechanism?
drill.a: Ticagrelor: adenosine accumulation. Usually mild and self-limiting (30% right).

drill.q: ACS with a recent TIA going for PCI: which P2Y12 inhibitor is contraindicated?
drill.a: Prasugrel (prior stroke or TIA).

drill.q: NSTEMI for early angiography, anatomy unknown: give a P2Y12 inhibitor now?
drill.a: No. Routine pretreatment is class III; defer to PCI (GT7 Q104). Aspirin yes.

drill.q: NSTE-ACS anticoagulant: angiography <24 h vs >24 h?
drill.a: <24 h: UFH (enoxaparin IIa). >24 h: fondaparinux (OASIS-5: half the major bleeding of enoxaparin). Fondaparinux alone in primary PCI: class III.

drill.q: NSTE-ACS, CrCl 24 mL/min: enoxaparin?
drill.a: 1 mg/kg ONCE daily. Reduced, not contraindicated (GT7 Q109).

drill.q: Urgent CABG: how long before do you stop eptifibatide? Ticagrelor?
drill.a: Eptifibatide/tirofiban 2-4 h (GT7 Q116). Ticagrelor or clopidogrel ≥24 h. Elective: ticagrelor 3, clopidogrel 5, prasugrel 7 days.

drill.q: NSTE-ACS angiography timing: very high risk, high risk?
drill.a: Very high risk (shock, refractory pain, acute HF, arrhythmia): <2 h, class I. High risk (NSTEMI, GRACE >140, dynamic ST-T): <24 h, now IIa.

drill.q: GRACE vs TIMI: what does each predict, and which counts aspirin use?
drill.a: GRACE: death (>140 high risk). TIMI: death/MI/urgent revascularisation at 14 days; aspirin in the last 7 days adds a point.

drill.q: VT or NSVT 48 h after a large MI: mechanism? And sustained VT 2 years later?
drill.a: Abnormal automaticity at 24-72 h. Scar re-entry weeks to years later. AIVR = enhanced normal automaticity, benign.

drill.q: Complete heart block after anterior MI: level, escape, treatment?
drill.a: Infranodal (His-Purkinje), wide escape <40/min, atropine-resistant: transvenous pacing. Inferior MI: nodal, narrow escape, usually transient.

drill.q: Killip classes?
drill.a: I no HF; II S3 or crackles <50% of lung fields; III frank pulmonary oedema; IV cardiogenic shock.

drill.q: Inferior STEMI, new murmur, pulmonary oedema, cold and hypotensive: which intervention next?
drill.a: IABP (IIa for mechanical complications; lowers afterload), then surgery. Not norepinephrine (38% right). Routine IABP in shock is class III.

drill.q: Sudden PEA with tamponade days after a large STEMI?
drill.a: LV free wall rupture.

drill.q: ST elevation still present 6 weeks after anterior MI, Q waves, no troponin rise?
drill.a: LV aneurysm. Risk: apical thrombus → anticoagulate.

drill.q: After MI with EF 32%: which long-term drugs are class I?
drill.a: ACE inhibitor (GT8 Q26) and β-blocker; MRA if HF or diabetes; statin and 12-month DAPT for all. Not milrinone, digoxin or nitrates.

questions.text: Unstable or stable: the tachycardia algorithm and the shock

steps.bridge: Unstable means a shock. But this heart is still beating, so the shock has to be timed.

lesson.text:
Every fast rhythm you'll ever be shown starts with the same question, and it isn't what the rhythm is. It's whether the rhythm is hurting the patient.

Start with why a fast heart fails at all. The heart fills in diastole, and the coronary arteries fill in diastole too. As the rate climbs, systole hardly shortens, so it's diastole that gets squeezed. The ventricle fills less, so output falls. The muscle is fed less, at the very moment it's working hardest. You met those in the shock packets as filling and pump. A tachycardia attacks both.

So the algorithm lists five signs that this has happened. Hypotension. Acutely altered mental status. Signs of shock. Ischaemic chest discomfort. Acute heart failure. Three of them are low output, one is the starved coronary, and one is pressure backing up into the lung.

[[Unstable means hypotension, acutely altered mental status, signs of shock, ischaemic chest discomfort or acute heart failure, caused by the rhythm. Any one of them means synchronised cardioversion.]]

If any one is present, the answer is electricity: a synchronised cardioversion. Why not a drug? Because a shock works in a single beat and doesn't depress the heart, while a drug takes minutes and most of them lower the pressure further. There's one permitted alternative. If the rhythm is regular and narrow, adenosine may be considered, because that rhythm is probably a circuit through the AV node and adenosine breaks it in seconds.

If none of the five is present, you have time. Take a twelve-lead ECG, secure IV access, and then measure the QRS. Under zero point one two seconds is narrow, which means the ventricles are being activated down the normal His-Purkinje wiring, so the rhythm starts above them. Zero point one two seconds or more is wide, and a wide tachycardia is VT until proved otherwise.

Now the way the bank asks it. The lowest score on this card, thirty per cent, was a man with recurrent palpitations, no chest pain, no breathlessness, and AF on the ECG. The tempting option was to sedate him and cardiovert at one hundred joules. He has symptoms, but none of the five signs. NEET's favourite wrong option here is the shock for a patient who is merely symptomatic. He's stable, and stable AF gets rate control with diltiazem or a beta-blocker.

The reverse error appears too. A pressure of seventy-five over forty, a rate of one hundred and eighty, a regular broad QRS: cardiovert. One Marrow key chose intubation for an unstable wide tachycardia, but only because cardioversion wasn't among the options. If it's offered, take it.

And one paediatric line, asked directly. A child's SVT converts with adenosine, returns within seconds, and now the child is unstable. More adenosine buys another thirty seconds. The answer is synchronised cardioversion at half to one joule per kilogram, then two joules per kilogram. Never verapamil or diltiazem in an infant, because they cause cardiovascular collapse.

So the first fork is settled: unstable, shock. But what makes this shock different from the one you give in an arrest?

steps.bridge: You know when the shock lands. Next, how much energy each rhythm needs under the current guideline.

lesson.text:
You've just chosen a shock for a heart that's still beating. That's the whole difference between cardioversion and defibrillation, and it comes down to timing.

Think about what a beating ventricle is doing through one cycle. At the R wave the whole ventricle has just been depolarised and is refractory. A shock landing there finds nothing excitable to disturb except the circuit you're trying to break. On the upslope of the T wave it's different. Some of the muscle has recovered and some hasn't. Excitable tissue lying beside refractory tissue is exactly the ground re-entry needs, and a shock that lands there can start VF. That's the R on T phenomenon.

So the machine is told to watch for the R wave and fire on its peak. That's synchronisation.

[[Cardioversion is synchronised to the peak of the R wave, so the shock can't fall on the T wave and cause VF. Defibrillation is unsynchronised, because VF and polymorphic VT have no reliable R wave to find.]]

Which rhythms get which follows from that. If there's an organised QRS, synchronise: VT with a pulse, AF, flutter. If there isn't, you can't. VF has no R wave at all, and polymorphic VT changes shape from beat to beat, so the machine may lock onto a T wave or never fire. Both are defibrillated.

The trap is simple: synchronised to the T wave, or to the P wave. It's the R wave. The T wave is precisely what you're avoiding.

So you know when the shock lands. Next, how big it should be.

steps.bridge: Timing and energy are set. Now the bedside: who is shocked at once, and what must be ready.

lesson.text:
The timing is fixed. Now the size of the shock, and here the twenty twenty-five guideline changed the numbers. That matters, because two bank keys still carry the old ones.

Start with why different rhythms need different energies. A shock ends an arrhythmia by depolarising enough muscle at once that the circuit has nowhere left to go. How much current that takes depends on how much tissue is involved. AF is many small wavelets wandering across both atria, so you have to capture a large mass of atrium in one go. Flutter is one large circuit in the atrium. A regular SVT is a small circuit through the node. Monomorphic VT is one organised ventricular circuit with a clean R wave.

The old teaching was to start low and climb. What changed is the evidence on starting low. Low-energy shocks failed more often, and worse, they sometimes provoked the next arrhythmia: VF when cardioverting AF, and AF when cardioverting flutter. A failed shock isn't free. It means another shock under sedation, more delay, and another chance of harm. Pooled biphasic trials found that two hundred joules gave over ninety per cent cumulative success, with no extra myocardial injury.

{{**AHA 2025, synchronised, biphasic**
AF | at least 200 J (class 2a)
Flutter | 200 J (class 2b)
Narrow regular SVT | 100 J
Monomorphic VT with a pulse | 100 J
Polymorphic VT | unsynchronised, defibrillation dose (class 1)}}

[[From twenty twenty-five, AF starts at two hundred joules or more and flutter at two hundred. Narrow regular SVT and monomorphic VT with a pulse start at one hundred. Sustained polymorphic VT is defibrillated, unsynchronised.]]

One point of honesty about the hundred. The guideline text gives a figure only for AF and flutter. The hundred joules for SVT and monomorphic VT comes from the algorithm chart, and it's what the keys use.

Now the traps. First, the old AF range. One grand test keys one hundred and twenty to two hundred joules for unstable AF, and a question bank item keys one hundred. In both, what's being tested is cardioversion over a drug, and that part is right. So pick cardioversion, and if two hundred or more is on the list, that's the current answer.

Second, polymorphic VT with a pulse. NEET's favourite wrong options are synchronised cardioversion at one hundred joules, and magnesium. The guideline treats every sustained polymorphic VT as unstable, whatever the QT, and gives an immediate unsynchronised shock. Magnesium belongs to one situation: torsades on a long QT that comes in runs and stops by itself. You'll meet it properly in the wide section.

You may see European numbers in a stem: maximum output for AF, seventy to one hundred and twenty joules for flutter and SVT, one hundred and twenty to one hundred and fifty for VT with a pulse. The bank keys follow the American numbers, so learn the box.

You've got the timing and the dose. What's left is the bedside: who gets shocked at once, and what you need around you.

steps.bridge: Now the whole section in one patient: fast AF, low pressure, wet lungs, duration unknown.

lesson.text:
Timing, energy, and now the doing of it. Four things on this card, and the questions come from three of them.

First, when to prepare to shock at once. The algorithm's number is a ventricular rate above one hundred and fifty. Why a rate? Because a reasonably healthy heart tolerates anything slower. If a patient is hypotensive at a rate of one hundred and twenty, the rhythm is very unlikely to be the cause. Something else is, sepsis or bleeding or hypoxia, and the heart is racing to compensate. Shocking a compensatory sinus tachycardia does nothing at all. So below about one hundred and fifty, look for the cause and treat that.

Second, what's at the bedside: a saturation monitor, suction, an IV line and intubation equipment. Each one answers a specific risk. Sedation can stop breathing or cause aspiration, and the shock itself can leave a bradycardia or VF.

Third, the prerequisites: consent, sedation and analgesia, and ruling out a left atrial clot. Take sedation first, because it was asked. The current guidance is that sedation is advisable in the awake patient, judged against how stable he is, and it must never dangerously delay the shock. The trap options are mandatory intubation, or an arterial line, before cardioversion. Neither is required, and both delay it.

Now the clot, which is the part asked most. In AF the atria don't contract, blood stagnates in the left atrial appendage, and after about forty-eight hours you must assume a clot has formed. Restore sinus rhythm and the atrium may throw it into the brain. So for AF of more than forty-eight hours, or of unknown duration, in a stable patient, you anticoagulate for three weeks first, or you look with a transoesophageal echo and cardiovert if the appendage is clear. Then comes the half people forget. After sinus rhythm returns on the ECG, the atrium is stunned and contracts poorly for weeks. New clot can still form.

[[Before elective cardioversion of AF beyond forty-eight hours: three weeks of anticoagulation, or a transoesophageal echo. After it: at least four weeks, whatever the stroke score, because the atrium stays stunned.]]

NEET's favourite wrong option is two or three weeks after. Three is the number before. Four is the number after, and seventy-eight per cent got it. Only then does the stroke score decide the long term.

And none of that applies to the unstable patient. Shock first, heparin alongside. The next card is exactly that patient.

Fourth, two procedural notes. Resynchronise after each shock, because many machines drop back to unsynchronised mode once they've fired. And if the machine can't find an R wave and the patient is crashing, don't wait: give an unsynchronised shock.

Now put the whole section into one patient.

steps.bridge: The unstable limb is done. From here the patient is stable, and the first rhythm is narrow and regular.

lesson.text:
Here's the section in a single stem. AF at one hundred and sixty. Pressure eighty-four over fifty. Basal crackles, saturation eighty-eight per cent. Duration unknown, not anticoagulated. Next step?

Run it the way you've just learned. Is the rhythm causing harm? At one hundred and sixty the ventricle has too little diastole to fill, and in AF the atrial kick that tops it up has gone. Output falls: that's the hypotension. Left atrial pressure rises behind a ventricle that can't fill, and that's the crackles and the falling saturation. Two of the five signs, and a rate above one hundred and fifty. He's unstable, and the rhythm is the reason.

So the answer is immediate synchronised cardioversion. The examiner has put three distractors in front of you, and each is something you'd rightly do for a different patient.

The first is rate control: IV diltiazem or metoprolol. Both are negative inotropes, and diltiazem dilates vessels as well. In a patient who's already hypotensive and wet, they can cause an arrest. On the mini test only forty-eight per cent chose the shock.

The second is the clot rule: heparin and delayed cardioversion, or a transoesophageal echo first. Duration unknown, not anticoagulated: it looks like the three-week patient from the last card. But those rules protect a stable patient from an elective procedure. In shock, waiting is the greater risk.

[[Unstable AF: shock now, with heparin started alongside. The three weeks and the transoesophageal echo are for the stable patient. They never delay an emergency cardioversion.]]

The third is amiodarone.
